newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Financing woes hit CITIC after China Light deal.
newsitem.headline: Financing woes hit CITIC after China Light deal.

text.p: CITIC Pacific Ltd's stake in China Light should give the conglomerate an immediate earnings boost, but the short-term concern for investors is how the purchase will be funded, analysts said on Wednesday.

Investors sold down CITIC Pacific shares after the company said on Tuesday it would buy 497.66 million new shares, or 20 percent of China Light & Power Co Ltd's enlarged share capital, at HK$32.66 per share.
CITIC Pacific shares fell HK$1.00 to HK$38.50 on Wednesday.
"You have a good partner with quality earnings to add to the CITIC base but there will be a fund-raising need for this acquisition," said Herbert Lau, an analyst at Vickers Ballas.
CITIC said on Tuesday it would fund the HK$16.25 billion purchase with internal resources and bank borrowings.
But analysts said there was also the possibility of a share placement or a sale of some of CITIC's stake in Hong Kong Telecommunications Ltd.
"It is quite a good medium- to long-term strategy to have a stake in China Light and the acquisition price is reasonable," said Ben Kwong, director of research at Dharmala Securities.
"But the problem is that the move involves HK$16 billion and that will have a burden on the company's financial position."
Funding the acquisition through bank debt would increase the company's gearing substantially, analysts said.
"We estimate that it will be around 70 percent," said Lau, adding that current gearing was about 30 percent.
Edward Chan, head of research at Amsteel Securities, said if CITIC funded the whole purchase with bank debt, its gearing would rise to about 90 percent.

"It is quite unlikely that CITIC is going to finance this purchase with 100 percent borrowings so there could be some speculation on whether CITIC will place more shares to raise funds or dispose of some other investment holdings within the group like the remaining eight percent in Hongkong Telecom," Chan said.
He said disposing of the entire Hongkong Telecom stake would raise about HK$12 billion.
"There are still other options that they can consider such as disposing of some non-core assets. It has been rumoured that they are going to spin off the motor vehicle operations," Kwong said.
"In the medium term, the China infrastructure projects will also be be spun off."
ING Barings research director Mark Simpson said whatever the choice of financing, the benefits of the deal should offset the negative financing impact.
He upgraded his earnings per share estimates for CITIC Pacific to HK$2.29 for 1997, up three percent from his previous estimate, and to HK$2.98 from HK$2.65 for 1998.
"I think the benefits to earnings per share and net asset value outweigh the short-term concerns about debt," he said.

"One would expect over time that the market will perceive that China Light can move away from poor growth of its core generating operations in Hong Kong and seek faster growth opportunities by exploiting the China market," Simpson said.
Chan said China Light's joint residential development project with Cheung Kong (Holdings) Ltd in Hok Un in Kowloon should contribute to earnings.
"It is going to be a very major project between 1998 and 2001. I think this project will fetch profit of some HK$11 billion for China Light," he said.
But some analysts said it was difficult to see the immediate benefits China Light would bring to CITIC Pacific.
"We are still waiting for major plans to be announced so we are waiting to see the synergies," said Amy Wong, research director at New China Hong Kong Securities Ltd.
